I mostly felt that way too, but over the last couple of days something that helped me a lot is trying to think "how do I manage an employee" when thinking about Dot. When I was a manager it would never have worked if I just tried to track everything in a single DM inbox with each of my engineers, so I just shouldn't try to do the same thing with Dot.
If Dot was another person that I was working with on a bunch of things, I'd try to use tools like task managers (e.g. todoist) and knowledge bases (e.g. notion) to keep track of what they're up to, what they did, what they delivered, what's still open, what needs my attention, etc. We'd dm each other when we need to, but we wouldn't try to make this the only way we'd organise stuff. 
So I've started doing the same thing with Elminster (my Dot), and so far it seems to work pretty well. We have a notion workspace where Elminster documents where things are on different projects, their next steps, blockers, decisions needed from me, etc. As unfathomably corporate brain as it sounds I have daily 1:1s with him to get an overview of where things stand and what's next.
It's VERY far from perfect, but it works *much* better than it did when I just tried to talk to him to the Dots single chat. Really recommend people to try this reframe and see what you think.

Oh yes, I know! I tried to use Dots to steer Codex and it was a nightmare. 

I ended up having to setup a custom tunnel MCP so my Dot can tunnel into my Mac and drive agents via the Paseo MCP. It works better than its native Codex orchestration, but still wasn’t great (it doesn’t know how to prompt agents! It talks to external agents like its own internal thinking trace and as if those agents share its context window), so I stopped doing that.

Grok Bot is better but it eats tokens like crazy. Still figuring out my setup there but it at least reliably reacts to a Tibo reset and then burns it down to 0 as quickly as possible before the next reset. 

The best coordinator setup I found so far is Claude Projects. Lot of rough edges now since it’s beta (especially around permissions), but I feel the most productive in it. 

Especially when you lean into using Artifacts to review work and make decisions.

YOU ARE PAYING SENIOR RATES TO RENAME FILES

the setup everyone is reposting is OpenAI Dots plus Claude Code as one dev team. the part actually worth stealing is smaller than that: which model gets the task first.

Sonnet 5.5 reads at $2 per million and writes at $10. Opus 5.5 is double on both.

~/project-x $ claude -p "Fix issue #381. Run the tests. Open a pull request." --model claude-sonnet-5-5

here's the split:

▸ Sonnet takes the first pass on everything, 2 tries maximum
▸ Opus gets it only when Sonnet is stuck, 1 try, and it plans instead of typing
▸ tests decide, not the model. 318 of 318 or the task is not done
▸ you approve the pull request, and nothing merges itself

on 1,000 tasks that is roughly $480 instead of $800 for the same work, because the expensive brain only wakes up for the 20% that earns it.

the part that makes this safe: the Dot never merges. it opens the issue, reads the result and writes you a summary. the branch, the commits and the test output all live in GitHub, so neither model has to remember anything.

by 08:00 there is a PR waiting with no database changes and your approval missing, not a commit you have to undo.

the benchmarks are closer than that price gap suggests. Sonnet beats Opus on Terminal-Bench 4.0, 70.6 to 66.4. Opus pulls ahead on the long messy ones, FrontierCode 54.4 to 46.2. that spread is the entire reason a router exists.

one honest warning: there is no connect button. OpenAI and Anthropic ship nothing that joins these two. you build the GitHub bridge yourself, and if your tests are weak you have only automated a bad merge faster.

8 hours of nothing becomes 9 tasks routed, fixed and green before you open the laptop.

save it, this is the cheapest senior engineer you will ever avoid hiring.
